conversion_quality.interpretation: Measures conversion/extraction quality, not whether the source literature itself is scientifically correct.

claim_readouts.assertion_text: How can we support the production of machine-readable expressions of research findings in the data analysis phase of the research lifecycle?
claim_readouts.current_read: No evidence link is attached; the claim needs evidence.

claim_readouts.assertion_text: The authors propose a pre-publication approach (reborn) that produces machine-readable expressions of research findings during data analysis, using ORKG templates to specify formal data syntax for statistical findings.

evidence_for.rationale: Implementation of the soil science use case demonstrates that the reborn approach is implementable in R and produces reborn data.
evidence_for.evidence_text: Soil science use case (Gentsch et al., SOIL 2024): the authors integrated ORKG templates with the original R scripts to produce reborn data for descriptive statistics, LMM fittings, pairwise t-tests, and structural equation modeling, deposited at https://doi.org/10.48366/R664252 and interlinked with the article DOI via DataCite IsSupplementTo.

evidence_for.rationale: Listing 1 supplies a working Python example of the proposed template-based production workflow.
evidence_for.evidence_text: Listing 1 shows a working Python example that materializes ORKG template R12002 (Student's t-test) and writes a JSON-LD reborn data file with label, dependent variable, input dataset, and output p-value.

claim_readouts.assertion_text: The reborn approach is superior to classical manual and semi-automated post-publication extraction in terms of knowledge accuracy, richness, reproducibility, and technological simplicity.

evidence_for.rationale: Table 1 makes the comparative claim explicit by scoring pre-publication production highest on Accuracy/Richness/Simplicity.
evidence_for.evidence_text: Table 1 qualitative comparison: pre-publication production gets two-checkmark (best) scores for Accuracy, Richness, and Simplicity, but lags (X) on Scalability and Legacy versus automated post-publication extraction.

evidence_for.rationale: Author-cited literature shows automated extraction lags on accuracy except on the simplest tasks, supporting the comparative superiority claim on accuracy.
evidence_for.evidence_text: Cited performance figures for automated post-publication extraction: ~90% accuracy for TDM extraction (Kabongo et al. 2021); 91.6% for LLM materials-data extraction (Polak & Morgan 2024); ~60% keyphrase identification, ~40% classification, ~30% relation extraction (Augenstein et al. 2017); 90-95% only on simplest tasks (Jonnalagadda et al. 2015).

mixed_or_inconclusive.rationale: The acknowledged scope limitation (only statistical knowledge, only scripting languages) qualifies the claim that reborn is superior overall.
mixed_or_inconclusive.evidence_text: Author-stated argument in the Limitations subsection: the approach has not been tested on qualitative knowledge, formulae, proofs, or arguments, and remains tied to scripting languages (R/Python) rather than commercial GUI-driven tools.

mixed_or_inconclusive.rationale: Author-reliance limits coverage of reborn output, qualifying claims of overall superiority.
mixed_or_inconclusive.evidence_text: Author-stated argument that the system's coverage depends on authors choosing which findings to express in machine-readable form and may miss results authors deem trivial but others find important.

claim_readouts.assertion_text: The reborn approach was applied to three use cases (soil science by Gentsch et al., computer science by Thießen et al., agroecology by Perez-Alvarez et al.) and produced machine-readable research findings in each, demonstrating practical viability.

evidence_for.rationale: The soil science use case is one of the three concrete deployments and is described in detail (production, deposition, collection).
evidence_for.evidence_text: Soil science use case (Gentsch et al., SOIL 2024): the authors integrated ORKG templates with the original R scripts to produce reborn data for descriptive statistics, LMM fittings, pairwise t-tests, and structural equation modeling, deposited at https://doi.org/10.48366/R664252 and interlinked with the article DOI via DataCite IsSupplementTo.

evidence_for.rationale: The CS use case provides a second concrete deployment producing reborn TDMS data.
evidence_for.evidence_text: Computer science use case (Thießen et al., NLP4KGC 2023): TDMS-tuples for synonym discovery on SciERC were captured with the ORKG Leaderboard template (F1 scores: SciBERT 0.713, BART 0.668, RoBERTa 0.657), reborn data deposited at https://doi.org/10.48366/R661500; produced retroactively as the CEUR-WS article has no DOI.

evidence_for.rationale: The agroecology use case provides the third concrete deployment with retroactive reborn-data production.
evidence_for.evidence_text: Agroecology use case (Perez-Alvarez et al., Ecological Applications 2018): retroactive production of reborn data for LMM fittings and linear regressions, deposited at https://doi.org/10.48366/R689181 and discovered via the article DOI through ORKG harvesting.

claim_readouts.assertion_text: Automated post-publication extraction of scientific knowledge currently achieves high accuracy (above 90-95%) only for the simplest tasks (e.g. TDM tuples, ~90%), and accuracy drops substantially (60% keyphrase identification, 40% classification, 30% relation extraction) for more general tasks.

evidence_for.rationale: The cited performance figures directly underpin the background claim about current automated-extraction accuracy.
evidence_for.evidence_text: Cited performance figures for automated post-publication extraction: ~90% accuracy for TDM extraction (Kabongo et al. 2021); 91.6% for LLM materials-data extraction (Polak & Morgan 2024); ~60% keyphrase identification, ~40% classification, ~30% relation extraction (Augenstein et al. 2017); 90-95% only on simplest tasks (Jonnalagadda et al. 2015).

claim_readouts.assertion_text: By embedding expressive data type schemata into data analysis, the reborn approach delivers richer, more granular machine-readable expressions of scientific knowledge than either manual or automated post-publication extraction can.

evidence_for.rationale: Table 1 explicitly scores pre-publication production highest on Richness vs. both manual and automated post-publication extraction.
evidence_for.evidence_text: Table 1 qualitative comparison: pre-publication production gets two-checkmark (best) scores for Accuracy, Richness, and Simplicity, but lags (X) on Scalability and Legacy versus automated post-publication extraction.

claim_readouts.assertion_text: Reborn data can strengthen the peer-review process by giving reviewers structured, finer-grained access to research findings and by enabling verification of figures and reproducibility of scripts.

evidence_for.rationale: The soil science use case demonstrates interlinked scripts/data that could be made available to reviewers, illustrating the peer-review benefit (though not formally evaluated).
evidence_for.evidence_text: Soil science use case (Gentsch et al., SOIL 2024): the authors integrated ORKG templates with the original R scripts to produce reborn data for descriptive statistics, LMM fittings, pairwise t-tests, and structural equation modeling, deposited at https://doi.org/10.48366/R664252 and interlinked with the article DOI via DataCite IsSupplementTo.

claim_readouts.assertion_text: The reborn approach has been developed and evaluated only for statistical/quantitative knowledge in R and Python computing environments; it has not been tested on qualitative or other knowledge types (formulae, proofs, arguments), nor on commercial environments without scripting (SPSS, GraphPad, Stata).

evidence_for.rationale: The Limitations subsection states this scope restriction directly.
evidence_for.evidence_text: Author-stated argument in the Limitations subsection: the approach has not been tested on qualitative knowledge, formulae, proofs, or arguments, and remains tied to scripting languages (R/Python) rather than commercial GUI-driven tools.

claim_readouts.assertion_text: ORKG templates specify only data syntax and do not encode formal semantics, so reborn data cannot currently support reasoning and only partially meet the FAIR interoperability sub-principles.

evidence_for.rationale: The Limitations subsection states the syntax-only template limitation directly.
evidence_for.evidence_text: Author-stated argument that ORKG templates capture only syntax (no formal semantics), limiting interoperability and reasoning support, with mitigation via mappings to ontologies like STATO.

claim_readouts.assertion_text: The reborn approach inherits an adoption/scalability limitation: it relies on authors to apply it during the research lifecycle, so coverage depends on researcher uptake and on which results authors choose to express.

evidence_for.rationale: The Limitations subsection states the author-reliance limitation directly.
evidence_for.evidence_text: Author-stated argument that the system's coverage depends on authors choosing which findings to express in machine-readable form and may miss results authors deem trivial but others find important.

claim_readouts.assertion_text: If pre-publication production approaches such as reborn are adopted, reliance on post-publication extraction is predicted to decline in the coming decades and may become largely obsolete in the second half of the century.

evidence_for.rationale: The Zenodo analysis is used to argue that adoption is plausible and growing, indirectly supporting the speculative impact claim.
evidence_for.evidence_text: A quick analysis of approximately 90K Zenodo records showed that about 5K (~5%) contain Python or R files and are interlinked in metadata to about 8K published articles, indicating that hundreds-to-thousands of articles could be interlinked with reborn data in the coming years.

claim_readouts.assertion_text: The proposed distributed system uses a (statistical) Computing Environment plus Library, a Data Type Registry of templates (implemented in ORKG), a Publisher and Data Repository for reborn data, and Aggregation Systems (e.g. ORKG) that discover reborn data via DOI metadata.

evidence_for.rationale: Methods section and Fig. 6 directly describe the components and interactions of the distributed system.
evidence_for.evidence_text: Architectural overview (Fig. 6) and Methods section describe a working distributed system: computing environment + ORKG Python/R library + ORKG template registry + TIB Leibniz Data Manager repository + ORKG aggregation system, with DataCite/Crossref DOI-metadata interlinking (Listings 2-4) and DOI/directory harvesting (Listing 5).
